desc:
Start with an empty binary search tree and insert the distinct integers of values one after another, in the given order. Every insertion uses the standard rule: begin at the root, go left when the new value is smaller than the current node and right when it is larger, and attach the new node at the first missing child. The first value becomes the root.

Return an array d where d[i] is the depth of values[i] at the moment it is inserted (the root has depth 0, its children depth 1, and so on). Nodes never move afterwards, so this is also its final depth.

Doing the insertions one by one can take O(n2) time when the sequence is sorted; try to do better.

Example 1

values = [5,2,8,1,3]
Output: [0,1,1,2,2]

Example 2

values = [1,2,3,4]
Output: [0,1,2,3]
The tree is a path.

Example 3

values = [4,6,5,7,3]
Output: [0,1,2,2,1]
hints: The depth of a new node is one more than the depth of its parent. Which existing node will become the parent of the new value?
When a value is inserted, its parent is either the predecessor or the successor of the value among the values already inserted: whichever of the two was inserted later (is deeper).

Finding the predecessor and successor among earlier values is easy if you go backwards: put all values in a doubly linked list sorted by value, then remove them from the last insertion to the first. At the moment you remove values[i], its two list neighbours are exactly its neighbours among values[0..i-1]. Then compute depths forwards: d[i] = 1 + max(d[pred], d[succ]).
editorial: Claim: when x is inserted, its parent is its predecessor or its successor among the values already in the tree, namely the one inserted later. Both are on the search path of x, and between them in value order there is nothing else yet. Hence depth(x) = 1 + max(depth(pred), depth(succ)) (a missing neighbour counts as depth -1, which makes the first element depth 0).

To get pred and succ among earlier elements for all i at once, sort the indices by value and link them in a doubly linked list. Process i from n-1 down to 0: the neighbours of i in the list right now are the closest earlier-inserted values around values[i] (all later ones have been removed already); record them and unlink i in O(1). Then fill the depths forwards in insertion order. Total O(n log n) for the sort and O(n) for the rest, with no tree needed.
